the risk of a cancer of one of the three sites was elevated following a cancer of one or both of the other sites.

women who have had a breast cancer have a three- to four-fold increased risk of a cancer in the opposite breast, and an elevated risk of cancer of corpus uteri (RR = 2.1) and ovarian cancer (RR =1.5) within 1 year of diagnosis.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
breast cancer increases the risk of breast, corpus uteri and ovarian cancer, and that cancers of the corpus and ovarian uteri increase the risk of breast and ovarian cancer.

the risk of cancer at a site is increased after the diagnosis of a primary cancer at the other site, with the exception of the risk of ovarian cancer after a corpus uteri cancer, and the risk of breast cancer after a corpus uterus cancer in the Connecticut data.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the increased risk for a second cancer is highest for the breast, followed by the corpus uteri.
the risk of cancer in the contralat-eral breast is elevated following cancers of all three organs.
the risk of a contralateral breast cancer is increased following breast cancer and that a subsequent cancer of the corpus or ovary is more common than expected by chance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women who have had a cancer of the breast, corpus uteri or ovary are at increased risk of developing other cancers in these organs.
breast, endometrial and ovarian cancers share common aetiological factors and are often part of a spectrum of gynaecological cancers.

the increased risk of a second cancer in women with a history of breast cancer is not restricted to the contralateral or ipsilateral breast, but also includes cancers of the corpus and ovary, and vice versa.
